doc.title: Herbie Hancock interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 18, 1995

title: Winning the Young People's Concert and playing with the Chicago Symphony
summary: He won the audition, had to learn a new concerto, and later suspected the missing-parts story was untrue.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Now tell us about your debut with the symphony.

Well that was during the time that I was with Mrs. Jordan, the second teacher. By that time I was playing Bach inventions, some fugues and preludes and some Chopin. I had gotten into etudes and I think maybe Chopin’s “Fantasie Impromptu,” some things like that. So in 1950 — actually 1950, is that right? No — 1951 I auditioned for this — basically it was a concert. The Young People’s Concert Series in Chicago. And what would happen is that you would audition for who was then the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony. And that was George Schick, who became President of Manhattan School of Music later on by the way. Anyway, so they would select one person from each instrument of the orchestra who would be a winner, and I happened to win for the piano. And the prize would be to play a concerto with the Chicago Symphony. Anyway, I won. And then, well the way I found out that I won was that I received a post card in the mail about two months later, that said, “Congratulations, you’ve been selected as the piano winner of the Young People’s Concert Series, however,” — oh by the way, the date you are to perform is February 5, 1952 I think it was. Or 1951, I’ve forgotten. And maybe I auditioned in ‘50 and played in ‘51. But anyway, so anyway it said, “However the concerto that you auditioned with, somehow we haven’t been able to locate the orchestral parts, so you’ll either have to learn a new concerto or forfeit the performance just so you know you are a winner but you won’t be able to play with the Chicago Symphony.” So I had to learn a new concerto you know? And that other one I knew cold. The new one I had to learn in about three months so I didn’t have nearly as much time. And so I made the performance, and as a matter of fact after the performance I signed the first autograph that I ever signed, you know. But the next week — oh I should say that the performance was at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. And the next week my teacher had gotten herself and me tickets to see Myra Hess, who was a very famous classical pianist at the time, who was performing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So we went that week to see Myra Hess, guess what she played? The concerto that I auditioned with. So all of that nonsense that they said about not being able to find the parts was a bunch of bologna.
My teacher was mad. I thought she was going to tear that place up she was so mad. I mean she said to me, how could they do that to a little kid?
